                       "online_share": [0.62, 0.58, 0.81, 0.77, 0.30, 0.35, 0.85, 0.55, 0.28, 0.79],
                       "growth": [0.08, 0.07, 0.15, 0.14, 0.02, 0.03, 0.16, 0.09, 0.01, 0.13]},
                      index=["Pune", "Jaipur", "Bengaluru", "Hyderabad", "Patna", "Ranchi", "Mumbai", "Kochi", "Guwahati", "Chennai"])
Z = linkage(StandardScaler().fit_transform(cities), method="ward")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))
dendrogram(Z, labels=cities.index.tolist(), ax=ax, color_threshold=3)
ax.set_title("Cities merged step by step (Ward linkage) — cut the tree to choose clusters", fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
print({city: int(c) for city, c in zip(cities.index, fcluster(Z, t=3, criterion="maxclust"))})
{'Pune': 2, 'Jaipur': 2, 'Bengaluru': 1, 'Hyderabad': 1, 'Patna': 3, 'Ranchi': 3, 'Mumbai': 1, 'Kochi': 2, 'Guwahati': 3, 'Chennai': 1}

Agglomerative clustering starts with every point alone and repeatedly merges the closest pair. The dendrogram shows the whole merge history, so you can choose the number of clusters afterwards. Linkage defines "closest": ward (minimise variance increase, the usual default), average, complete or single.

DBSCAN: Arbitrary Shapes and Noise

Cell — where K-means failsPython
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
Xm, _ = make_moons(n_samples=500, noise=0.06, random_state=0)
Xm = np.vstack([Xm, rng.uniform(-1.5, 2.5, (25, 2))])                  # plus scattered noise points
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3))
axes[0].scatter(Xm[:, 0], Xm[:, 1], c=KMeans(2, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(Xm), cmap="coolwarm", s=6)
axes[0].set_title("K-means (k=2): cuts the moons in half", fontsize=9)
db = DBSCAN(eps=0.2, min_samples=8).fit(Xm)
axes[1].scatter(Xm[:, 0], Xm[:, 1], c=db.labels_, cmap="viridis", s=6)
axes[1].set_title(f"DBSCAN: {len(set(db.labels_)) - 1} clusters, {np.sum(db.labels_ == -1)} points marked noise", fontsize=9)
for ax in axes: ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout()
AlgorithmNeeds k?Cluster shapesScales toNotes
K-meansYesRound, similar sizeMillions (MiniBatchKMeans)Scale features; sensitive to outliers
HierarchicalNo (cut later)Depends on linkage~10,000sDendrogram is very explainable
DBSCAN / HDBSCANNoAny shape~100,000sFinds noise points; tune eps / min_samples
Gaussian mixtureYesElliptical, soft membershipMediumGives probabilities of membership
Clustering groups unlabelled data by similarity. K-means alternates assigning points to the nearest centroid and recomputing centroids to minimise inertia; it needs k (chosen with the elbow method, silhouette scores and business sense), scaled features and suits round, similar-sized clusters. Hierarchical agglomerative clustering merges closest groups using a linkage such as Ward and is visualised as a dendrogram cut at the desired level. DBSCAN finds dense regions of arbitrary shape and labels outliers as noise without specifying k. Gaussian mixtures give soft memberships. Clusters must be profiled and named to be actionable, as in RFM customer segmentation.
7.17

PCA & Dimensionality Reduction

Datasets often have dozens or thousands of correlated features. Principal Component Analysis finds new axes — principal components — that capture as much of the variation as possible, so a few components can stand in for many original features. It's used to compress data, speed up models, remove redundancy and visualise high-dimensional data in 2-D. (Module 3.7 showed the linear algebra: components are eigenvectors of the covariance matrix.)

The Idea in Two Dimensions

Cell — two strongly correlated features collapse to one directionPython
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
rng = np.random.default_rng(17)
height = rng.normal(170, 8, 300); weight = 0.9 * (height - 170) + 68 + rng.normal(0, 4, 300)
X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(np.c_[height, weight])
pca = PCA().fit(X)
print("explained variance ratio:", pca.explained_variance_ratio_.round(3))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.4))
ax.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], s=6, color="#8da0b2")
for vec, var, c in zip(pca.components_, pca.explained_variance_, ["#ffb454", "#6de5a0"]):
    ax.annotate("", xy=vec * 2 * np.sqrt(var), xytext=(0, 0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=c, lw=2.5))
ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlabel("height (scaled)"); ax.set_ylabel("weight (scaled)")
ax.set_title("PC1 (orange) follows the spread; PC2 is what's left", fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
explained variance ratio: [0.935 0.065]

How Many Components?

Cell — 64-pixel handwritten digitsPython
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
digits = load_digits()
Xd = digits.data                                                    # 1,797 images × 64 pixels
pca = PCA().fit(Xd)
cum = np.cumsum(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)
for target in (0.80, 0.90, 0.95, 0.99):
    print(f"{target:.0%} of variance kept with {np.argmax(cum >= target) + 1} of 64 components")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3))
axes[0].plot(np.arange(1, 65), cum, color="#4ea8de"); axes[0].axhline(0.95, ls=":", color="#8da0b2")
axes[0].set_xlabel("components"); axes[0].set_ylabel("cumulative variance"); axes[0].set_title("scree / cumulative plot", fontsize=9)
emb = PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(Xd)
sc = axes[1].scatter(emb[:, 0], emb[:, 1], c=digits.target, cmap="tab10", s=5)
axes[1].set_title("all 64 pixels projected onto 2 components (colour = digit)", fontsize=9)
plt.colorbar(sc, ax=axes[1], ticks=range(10))
plt.tight_layout()
80% of variance kept with 13 of 64 components 90% of variance kept with 21 of 64 components 95% of variance kept with 29 of 64 components 99% of variance kept with 41 of 64 components

Compression and Speed

Cell — reconstruct digits from few components; train fasterPython
import time
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.svm import SVC
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(9, 2))
for ax, k in zip(axes, (2, 8, 16, 32, 64)):
    p = PCA(n_components=k).fit(Xd)
    ax.imshow(p.inverse_transform(p.transform(Xd[:1])).reshape(8, 8), cmap="gray_r"); ax.set_title(f"{k} comps", fontsize=8); ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
for name, model in [("SVC on 64 pixels", SVC()), ("PCA(20) → SVC", make_pipeline(PCA(n_components=20), SVC()))]:
    t = time.perf_counter(); acc = cross_val_score(model, Xd, digits.target, cv=5).mean()
    print(f"{name:<18} accuracy {acc:.3f}  ({time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s)")
SVC on 64 pixels accuracy 0.963 (0.21s) PCA(20) → SVC accuracy 0.966 (0.16s)

Other Techniques

MethodTypeUse for
PCA / TruncatedSVDLinearCompression, de-correlation, pre-processing (SVD works on sparse text matrices)
t-SNE, UMAPNon-linear2-D visualisation of clusters (embeddings, images) — not for features; distances between clusters aren't meaningful
Autoencoders (Module 8)Non-linear, neuralCompression, anomaly detection
Feature selection (7.15)Keeps original columnsWhen interpretability matters
Scale features before PCA (otherwise large-unit features dominate), fit it on training data only (inside a pipeline), and remember components are blends of features — harder to explain than the originals.
Principal Component Analysis finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance — eigenvectors of the covariance matrix of standardised data — and projects data onto the first few, so correlated features compress into fewer components. The number of components is chosen from the cumulative explained-variance curve (for example 95%). PCA is used for compression, speeding up models, removing multicollinearity, noise reduction and 2-D visualisation; it must be fitted on training data inside a pipeline, requires scaling, and produces less interpretable features. Non-linear methods such as t-SNE and UMAP are for visualisation, and autoencoders provide neural compression.
7.18

Reinforcement Learning Basics

In reinforcement learning (RL) nobody gives the right answer. An agent takes actions in an environment, receives rewards, and learns a policy — what to do in each situation — that maximises total reward over time. It's how systems learned to play Go and Atari games, how robots learn to walk, and (as RLHF) how LLM assistants are tuned to be helpful.
Agent
chooses action a
→
Environment
moves to new state s′
→
Reward r
+ new state back to agent
TermMeaningDelivery-robot example
State sThe situationRobot's position in a warehouse grid
Action aA choiceMove up / down / left / right
Reward rImmediate feedback+10 at the packing desk, −10 into a hazard, −1 per step
Policy πState → action rule"From here, go right"
Discount γHow much future reward counts (0–1)0.9: reward now worth more than later
Exploration vs exploitationTry new actions vs use the best knownε-greedy: random move with probability ε

Q-Learning on a Grid

\[ Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha \Big[ r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a') - Q(s, a) \Big] \]Q(s, a): expected future reward for taking action a in state s · α: learning rate · the bracket is the "surprise" (temporal-difference error)
Cell — a warehouse robot learns the route by trial and errorPython
import numpy as np
grid = ["S...#",
        ".#.#.",
        ".#...",
        "...X.",
        "#.#.G"]            # S start, G packing desk (+10), X hazard (−10), # wall
rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
moves = {0: (-1, 0), 1: (1, 0), 2: (0, -1), 3: (0, 1)}          # up, down, left, right
arrows = {0: "↑", 1: "↓", 2: "←", 3: "→"}

def step(r, c, a):
    nr, nc = r + moves[a][0], c + moves[a][1]
    if not (0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols) or grid[nr][nc] == "#":
        nr, nc = r, c                                          # bumped into a wall: stay
    cell = grid[nr][nc]
    if cell == "G": return nr, nc, 10, True
    if cell == "X": return nr, nc, -10, True
    return nr, nc, -1, False

rng = np.random.default_rng(18)
Q = np.zeros((rows, cols, 4)); alpha, gamma, eps = 0.5, 0.9, 0.2
for episode in range(2000):
    r, c, done, steps = 0, 0, False, 0
    while not done and steps < 100:
        a = rng.integers(4) if rng.random() < eps else int(Q[r, c].argmax())     # explore or exploit
        nr, nc, reward, done = step(r, c, a)
        target = reward + (0 if done else gamma * Q[nr, nc].max())
        Q[r, c, a] += alpha * (target - Q[r, c, a])
        r, c, steps = nr, nc, steps + 1

print("learned policy:")
for i in range(rows):
    print(" ".join(grid[i][j] if grid[i][j] in "#GX" else arrows[int(Q[i, j].argmax())] for j in range(cols)))
r, c, path, done = 0, 0, [(0, 0)], False
while not done and len(path) < 20:
    r, c, _, done = step(r, c, int(Q[r, c].argmax())); path.append((r, c))
print("\ngreedy route from S:", path, f"— {len(path) - 1} steps, avoids the hazard")
learned policy: → → ↓ ← # ↑ # ↓ # ↓ ↑ # → → ↓ → → ↑ X ↓ # ↓ # ↑ G greedy route from S: [(0, 0), (0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2), (2, 2), (2, 3), (2, 4), (3, 4), (4, 4)] — 8 steps, avoids the hazard

No one told the robot the route. From rewards alone it learned to go around walls and the hazard by the shortest safe path.

Beyond Tables

  • Deep Q-Networks (DQN) replace the Q-table with a neural network for huge state spaces (pixels of a game screen)
  • Policy-gradient methods (PPO) learn the policy directly — used in robotics and RLHF for LLMs
  • Multi-armed bandits — the one-step special case — power A/B-test allocation, recommendations and ad selection
  • Practical libraries: Gymnasium (environments), Stable-Baselines3 (algorithms)
  • RL is data-hungry and hard to make safe; use it when actions change future states and a simulator exists
Reinforcement learning trains an agent to choose actions in an environment to maximise cumulative discounted reward, learning a policy from states, actions and rewards rather than labelled answers, while balancing exploration and exploitation (for example ε-greedy). Q-learning updates action values with the temporal-difference rule Q ← Q + α(r + γ·max Q′ − Q) and acts greedily on them; deep Q-networks approximate Q with neural networks, policy-gradient methods such as PPO optimise the policy directly and underpin RLHF, and multi-armed bandits handle one-step decisions like ad selection. RL needs simulators or lots of interaction and careful reward design.
7.19

Pipelines & Model Deployment Basics

A model in a notebook helps no one. To be useful it must accept new raw data and return predictions reliably — in a nightly batch job or a real-time API. A scikit-learn Pipeline bundles every preprocessing step with the model so training and prediction always do exactly the same thing. This lesson builds one, saves it, serves it, and covers what to monitor once it's live. (Module 10 goes deeper into MLOps.)

One Object from Raw Data to Prediction

Cell — ColumnTransformer + model in a PipelinePython
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(19)
n = 4000
raw = pd.DataFrame({"tenure_m": rng.integers(1, 72, n).astype(float), "monthly_bill": rng.normal(700, 250, n),
                    "support_calls": rng.poisson(1.2, n).astype(float),
                    "plan": rng.choice(["basic", "standard", "premium"], n), "city": rng.choice(["Hyd", "Blr", "Chn", "Pune"], n)})
logit = -0.6 - 0.05 * raw.tenure_m + 0.002 * raw.monthly_bill + 0.6 * raw.support_calls + (raw.plan == "basic") * 0.8
raw["churn"] = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))).astype(int)
raw.loc[rng.random(n) < 0.05, "monthly_bill"] = np.nan                     # real data has gaps

numeric, categorical = ["tenure_m", "monthly_bill", "support_calls"], ["plan", "city"]
pipe = Pipeline([
    ("prep", ColumnTransformer([
        ("num", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler())]), numeric),
        ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), categorical)])),
    ("model", HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=300, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=0)),
])
X, y = raw.drop(columns="churn"), raw.churn
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=0)
print("CV AUC:", cross_val_score(pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean().round(3))
pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(pipe)
CV AUC: 0.762 Pipeline(steps=[('prep', ColumnTransformer(transformers=[('num', Pipeline(steps=[('impute', SimpleImputer(strategy='median')), ('scale', StandardScaler())]), ['tenure_m', 'monthly_bill', 'support_calls']), ('cat', OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore'), ['plan', 'city'])])), ('model', HistGradientBoostingClassifier(learning_rate=0.05, max_iter=300, random_state=0))])

Because imputation, scaling and encoding live inside the pipeline, cross-validation re-fits them on each training fold (no leakage), and the same steps are applied automatically at prediction time.

Save, Load and Predict

Cell — persist the whole pipeline with its metadataPython
import joblib, json, sklearn, hashlib, os
joblib.dump(pipe, "churn_model_v1.joblib")
meta = {"model": "churn_model_v1", "trained_on_rows": len(X_train), "features": numeric + categorical,
        "sklearn_version": sklearn.__version__, "test_auc": None}
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
meta["test_auc"] = round(roc_auc_score(y_test, pipe.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]), 4)
meta["sha256"] = hashlib.sha256(open("churn_model_v1.joblib", "rb").read()).hexdigest()[:16]
json.dump(meta, open("churn_model_v1.json", "w"), indent=2)
print(json.dumps(meta, indent=2), f"\nfile size {os.path.getsize('churn_model_v1.joblib') // 1024} KB")

loaded = joblib.load("churn_model_v1.joblib")
new_customers = pd.DataFrame([{"tenure_m": 3, "monthly_bill": 1150, "support_calls": 4, "plan": "basic", "city": "Hyd"},
                              {"tenure_m": 48, "monthly_bill": 600, "support_calls": 0, "plan": "premium", "city": "Kochi"}])
print("churn probability:", loaded.predict_proba(new_customers)[:, 1].round(3), "← 'Kochi' was never seen; handled")
{ "model": "churn_model_v1", "trained_on_rows": 3200, "features": [ "tenure_m", "monthly_bill", "support_calls", "plan", "city" ], "sklearn_version": "1.9.1", "test_auc": 0.7351, "sha256": "b3bdbd838d79e514" } file size 1068 KB churn probability: [0.995 0.108] ← 'Kochi' was never seen; handled

Two Ways to Serve Predictions

Batch

A scheduled job scores all customers nightly and writes results to a table the CRM reads. Simple, cheap, easy to audit. Best when decisions aren't instant: churn lists, demand forecasts, lead scoring.

Real-time (online)

An API returns a prediction in milliseconds per request. Needed for fraud checks at payment, recommendations on page load, dynamic pricing.

Cell — a batch scoring job, and a FastAPI service (shown, not run here)Python
def score_batch(model_path: str, customers: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    model = joblib.load(model_path)
    out = customers[["city", "plan"]].copy()
    out["churn_prob"] = model.predict_proba(customers)[:, 1].round(4)
    out["risk_band"] = pd.cut(out.churn_prob, [0, 0.3, 0.6, 1], labels=["low", "medium", "high"])
    out["scored_at"] = pd.Timestamp("2026-11-18 02:00")
    return out

scored = score_batch("churn_model_v1.joblib", X_test)
print(scored.risk_band.value_counts().to_dict())

API_CODE = """
# app.py  —  run with:  uvicorn app:app --port 8000
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
import joblib, pandas as pd

app = FastAPI()
model = joblib.load("churn_model_v1.joblib")          # load once at start-up

class Customer(BaseModel):
    tenure_m: float
    monthly_bill: float | None = None
    support_calls: float
    plan: str
    city: str

@app.post("/predict")
def predict(c: Customer):
    p = model.predict_proba(pd.DataFrame([c.model_dump()]))[0, 1]
    return {"churn_probability": round(float(p), 4), "model": "churn_model_v1"}
"""
print(API_CODE.strip().splitlines()[0])
{'high': 316, 'low': 251, 'medium': 233} # app.py — run with: uvicorn app:app --port 8000

After Deployment: Monitor

Cell — detect data drift with the Population Stability IndexPython
def psi(expected, actual, bins=10):
    edges = np.quantile(expected, np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1)); edges[0], edges[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf
    e = np.histogram(expected, edges)[0] / len(expected); a = np.histogram(actual, edges)[0] / len(actual)
    e, a = np.clip(e, 1e-6, None), np.clip(a, 1e-6, None)
    return float(np.sum((a - e) * np.log(a / e)))

train_bill = X_train.monthly_bill.dropna()
this_month = rng.normal(700, 250, 2000)                    # same as training
after_price_rise = rng.normal(820, 260, 2000)               # tariffs went up
print(f"PSI this month:        {psi(train_bill, this_month):.3f}   (< 0.1 stable)")
print(f"PSI after price rise:  {psi(train_bill, after_price_rise):.3f}   (> 0.2 significant drift → investigate / retrain)")
PSI this month: 0.009 (< 0.1 stable) PSI after price rise: 0.276 (> 0.2 significant drift → investigate / retrain)
MonitorWhy
Input data quality and drift (PSI, missing rates, new categories)The world changes; the model was trained on the past
Prediction distributionA sudden jump in "high risk" share signals a problem
Actual performance once labels arrive (AUC, precision at the chosen threshold)Concept drift: relationships change
Latency, errors, costService health
Business outcome (churn actually reduced?)The point of the model
  • Version everything: data snapshot, code, model file, metrics (MLflow — Module 10)
  • Pin library versions; a pickle from one scikit-learn version may not load in another
  • Only load model files you trust — joblib/pickle can execute code when loaded (or use ONNX/skops formats)
  • Roll out gradually (shadow mode, then a canary), keep the previous model ready to roll back
A scikit-learn Pipeline with a ColumnTransformer bundles imputation, scaling, encoding and the model into one object, preventing leakage during cross-validation and guaranteeing identical preprocessing at prediction time; handle_unknown="ignore" protects against unseen categories. Pipelines are saved with joblib alongside metadata and library versions (loading only trusted files), then served in batch jobs that score records on a schedule or real-time APIs such as FastAPI. After deployment, models are monitored for data drift (for example PSI above 0.2), prediction shifts, live performance once labels arrive, service health and business impact, with versioning, gradual rollout and rollback.
7.20

End-to-End Project: Customer Churn

The brief: ConnectIN, a prepaid-heavy mobile and broadband provider with 1.2 million subscribers, loses roughly one in eight customers within any 30-day window. The retention team can contact 60,000 customers a month with a call and a ₹300 credit. Which customers should they call? This project runs the whole module: frame the problem, explore, build a leak-free pipeline, compare models with cross-validation, tune, pick a threshold by business value, test once, explain, and package.

1 · Frame the Problem

QuestionAnswer
PredictionProbability a customer cancels in the next 30 days (binary classification)
Decision it drivesWho gets a retention call; capacity 60,000 per month (5% of the base)
ValueSaved customer ≈ ₹4,800 margin (12 months × ₹400); call + credit ≈ ₹350; calls save ~30% of true churners
MetricROC-AUC / PR-AUC for model choice; net value of the top-ranked list for the decision
Baseline todayCall customers whose contract ends soonest

2 · Data

Cell — one row per customer, features as of the snapshot datePython
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(720)
n = 20_000
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "tenure_m": rng.integers(1, 96, n),
    "plan": rng.choice(["prepaid", "postpaid", "broadband", "bundle"], n, p=[0.35, 0.30, 0.15, 0.20]),
    "contract": rng.choice(["monthly", "annual", "two_year"], n, p=[0.55, 0.30, 0.15]),
    "monthly_bill": rng.lognormal(np.log(550), 0.4, n).round(),
    "data_gb_trend": rng.normal(0, 1, n).round(2),                  # change in data usage vs 3 months ago (z)
    "dropped_calls_30d": rng.poisson(2, n),
    "support_tickets_90d": rng.poisson(0.8, n),
    "late_payments_6m": rng.poisson(0.4, n),
    "months_to_contract_end": rng.integers(0, 24, n),
    "city_tier": rng.choice(["metro", "tier2", "tier3"], n, p=[0.5, 0.3, 0.2]),
    "has_app": rng.random(n) < 0.6,
})
df.loc[df.contract == "monthly", "months_to_contract_end"] = 0
df.loc[rng.random(n) < 0.04, "data_gb_trend"] = np.nan
logit = (-3.2 - 0.025 * df.tenure_m + 0.0012 * df.monthly_bill - 0.6 * df.data_gb_trend.fillna(0)
         + 0.18 * df.dropped_calls_30d + 0.45 * df.support_tickets_90d + 0.35 * df.late_payments_6m
         + df.contract.map({"monthly": 1.0, "annual": 0, "two_year": -0.8})
         + df.plan.map({"prepaid": 0.5, "postpaid": 0, "broadband": -0.2, "bundle": -0.7})
         - 0.4 * df.has_app + 0.6 * ((df.months_to_contract_end <= 1) & (df.contract != "monthly"))
         + 0.5 * (df.support_tickets_90d >= 3) * (df.tenure_m < 12))
df["churn_30d"] = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))).astype(int)
print(df.shape, f"churn rate {df.churn_30d.mean():.1%}")
print(df.head(3).to_string())

4 · Split and Pipeline

CellPython
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, StratifiedKFold, cross_validate
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
import lightgbm as lgb

X, y = df.drop(columns="churn_30d"), df.churn_30d
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=0)
num = ["tenure_m", "monthly_bill", "data_gb_trend", "dropped_calls_30d", "support_tickets_90d", "late_payments_6m", "months_to_contract_end"]
cat = ["plan", "contract", "city_tier", "has_app"]

def make_pipe(model, scale=True):
    num_steps = [("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"))] + ([("scale", StandardScaler())] if scale else [])
    prep = ColumnTransformer([("num", Pipeline(num_steps), num),
                              ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), cat)])
    return Pipeline([("prep", prep), ("model", model)])

candidates = {
    "logistic regression": make_pipe(LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)),
    "random forest": make_pipe(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=150, min_samples_leaf=20, n_jobs=-1, random_state=0), scale=False),
    "LightGBM": make_pipe(lgb.LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=400, learning_rate=0.03, num_leaves=31, min_child_samples=50,
                                             subsample=0.8, subsample_freq=1, colsample_bytree=0.8, verbose=-1, random_state=0), scale=False),
}
cv = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
for name, pipe in candidates.items():
    r = cross_validate(pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring=["roc_auc", "average_precision"], n_jobs=1)
    print(f"{name:<20} CV ROC-AUC {r['test_roc_auc'].mean():.4f} ± {r['test_roc_auc'].std():.4f}   PR-AUC {r['test_average_precision'].mean():.4f}")
logistic regression CV ROC-AUC 0.8025 ± 0.0122 PR-AUC 0.3951 random forest CV ROC-AUC 0.7874 ± 0.0116 PR-AUC 0.3583 LightGBM CV ROC-AUC 0.7821 ± 0.0075 PR-AUC 0.3532

5 · Improve: Features and Tuning

Cell — engineered features + a randomised search on LightGBMPython
from sklearn.model_selection import RandomizedSearchCV
from scipy.stats import loguniform, randint, uniform

def add_features(d):
    d = d.copy()
    d["renewal_window"] = ((d.months_to_contract_end <= 1) & (d.contract != "monthly")).astype(int)
    d["new_and_unhappy"] = ((d.tenure_m < 12) & (d.support_tickets_90d >= 3)).astype(int)
    d["bill_per_tenure"] = d.monthly_bill / (d.tenure_m + 1)
    return d
num_fe = num + ["renewal_window", "new_and_unhappy", "bill_per_tenure"]
Xtr_fe, Xte_fe = add_features(X_train), add_features(X_test)

prep_fe = ColumnTransformer([("num", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), num_fe),
                             ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), cat)])
lgb_pipe = Pipeline([("prep", prep_fe), ("model", lgb.LGBMClassifier(verbose=-1, random_state=0, subsample_freq=1, n_jobs=2))])
space = {"model__n_estimators": randint(200, 900), "model__learning_rate": loguniform(0.01, 0.1),
         "model__num_leaves": randint(8, 64), "model__min_child_samples": randint(20, 200),
         "model__subsample": uniform(0.6, 0.4), "model__colsample_bytree": uniform(0.6, 0.4),
         "model__reg_lambda": loguniform(1e-3, 10)}
search = RandomizedSearchCV(lgb_pipe, space, n_iter=8, cv=StratifiedKFold(3, shuffle=True, random_state=0), scoring="roc_auc", random_state=0, n_jobs=1).fit(Xtr_fe, y_train)
print(f"tuned LightGBM + features: CV ROC-AUC {search.best_score_:.4f}")
print({k.replace("model__", ""): (round(float(v), 4) if isinstance(v, float) else int(v)) for k, v in search.best_params_.items()})

lr_fe = Pipeline([("prep", ColumnTransformer([("num", Pipeline([("i", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("s", StandardScaler())]), num_fe),
                                              ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), cat)])),
                  ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000))])
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
print(f"logistic + features:       CV ROC-AUC {cross_val_score(lr_fe, Xtr_fe, y_train, cv=cv, scoring='roc_auc').mean():.4f}")
tuned LightGBM + features: CV ROC-AUC 0.7918 {'colsample_bytree': 0.719, 'learning_rate': 0.0114, 'min_child_samples': 160, 'n_estimators': 514, 'num_leaves': 9, 'reg_lambda': 1.4686, 'subsample': 0.8116} logistic + features: CV ROC-AUC 0.8026

A useful surprise: on this data plain logistic regression beats both tree ensembles, and tuning plus features lift LightGBM only to about the same level. The engineered features encode business knowledge (the renewal window, new customers with many complaints) that a linear model can't discover alone. When a simple model matches a complex one, choose the simple model — it's easier to explain, monitor and maintain. Gradient boosting usually wins when relationships are strongly non-linear; always let cross-validation decide.

6 · Decide by Business Value, then Test Once

Cell — value of calling the top-k customers, on held-out dataPython
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, average_precision_score
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict
VALUE_SAVED, SAVE_RATE, COST_CALL = 4800, 0.30, 350
final = lr_fe        # simpler model matched the tuned LightGBM in CV, so it wins (see note above)

def campaign_value(y_true, score, k):
    top = np.argsort(-score)[:k]
    churners = y_true.iloc[top].sum()
    return churners, churners * SAVE_RATE * VALUE_SAVED - k * COST_CALL

oof = cross_val_predict(final, Xtr_fe, y_train, cv=StratifiedKFold(3, shuffle=True, random_state=0), method="predict_proba")[:, 1]      # choose k on training folds
scale = 1_200_000 / len(y_train)                                                        # per-subscriber-base scaling
ks = np.arange(10_000, 300_001, 10_000)
values = [campaign_value(y_train, oof, int(k / scale))[1] * scale for k in ks]
k_best = ks[int(np.argmax(values))]
print(f"most valuable list size (scaled to 1.2M subscribers): {k_best:,} calls/month → capacity of 60,000 is {'binding' if k_best > 60000 else 'enough'}")

final.fit(Xtr_fe, y_train)                                                                # final fit, then ONE test evaluation
p_test = final.predict_proba(Xte_fe)[:, 1]
print(f"\nTEST  ROC-AUC {roc_auc_score(y_test, p_test):.4f}   PR-AUC {average_precision_score(y_test, p_test):.4f}  (base rate {y_test.mean():.3f})")
k = int(60_000 / 1_200_000 * len(y_test))
for name, score in [("model ranking", p_test), ("today's rule: contract ends soonest", -X_test.months_to_contract_end.to_numpy() + rng.random(len(X_test)) * 0.01),
                    ("random calls", rng.random(len(X_test)))]:
    caught, val = campaign_value(y_test, score, k)
    print(f"{name:<38} top {k} → churners reached {caught:>3} ({caught / k:.0%})  value ₹{val * 1_200_000 / len(y_test) / 1e5:,.1f} L/month")
most valuable list size (scaled to 1.2M subscribers): 140,000 calls/month → capacity of 60,000 is binding TEST ROC-AUC 0.8158 PR-AUC 0.4183 (base rate 0.118) model ranking top 200 → churners reached 110 (55%) value ₹265.2 L/month today's rule: contract ends soonest top 200 → churners reached 32 (16%) value ₹-71.8 L/month random calls top 200 → churners reached 21 (10%) value ₹-119.3 L/month

Cell — what drives predicted churn?Python
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
sample = Xte_fe.sample(2000, random_state=0)
perm = permutation_importance(final, sample, y_test.loc[sample.index], n_repeats=5, random_state=0, scoring="roc_auc")
imp = pd.Series(perm.importances_mean, index=sample.columns).sort_values()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6))
ax.barh(imp.index[-10:], imp.values[-10:], color="#4ea8de"); ax.set_title("Permutation importance (drop in test AUC)", loc="left", fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout()

one = Xte_fe.iloc[[int(np.argmax(p_test))]]
print("highest-risk customer:", f"p = {p_test.max():.2f}")
print(one[["tenure_m", "contract", "plan", "support_tickets_90d", "dropped_calls_30d", "data_gb_trend", "late_payments_6m"]].to_string(index=False))

Cell — model card summaryPython
import joblib
joblib.dump({"pipeline": final, "feature_fn": "add_features v1", "threshold_policy": "top 60,000 by probability"}, "connectin_churn_v1.joblib")
caught, val = campaign_value(y_test, p_test, k)
print(f"""MODEL CARD — ConnectIN churn v1
Purpose      Rank subscribers by 30-day churn risk for the retention call list (60,000/month)
Data         {len(X_train):,} training / {len(X_test):,} test customers, snapshot features only (no post-snapshot data)
Model        Logistic regression + 3 engineered features in a scikit-learn pipeline; tuned LightGBM
             scored no better in CV, so the simpler, explainable model was chosen
Performance  test ROC-AUC {roc_auc_score(y_test, p_test):.3f}; top-60,000 list reaches {caught / k:.0%} churners vs {y_test.mean():.0%} base rate
Value        ≈ ₹{val * 1_200_000 / len(y_test) / 1e5:,.1f} lakh net per month at current assumptions
Limits       Assumes 30% save rate (validate with a holdout A/B test); retrain monthly; monitor PSI on bill and usage
Owner        Retention analytics · review date 2027-02""")
MODEL CARD — ConnectIN churn v1 Purpose Rank subscribers by 30-day churn risk for the retention call list (60,000/month) Data 16,000 training / 4,000 test customers, snapshot features only (no post-snapshot data) Model Logistic regression + 3 engineered features in a scikit-learn pipeline; tuned LightGBM scored no better in CV, so the simpler, explainable model was chosen Performance test ROC-AUC 0.816; top-60,000 list reaches 55% churners vs 12% base rate Value ≈ ₹265.2 lakh net per month at current assumptions Limits Assumes 30% save rate (validate with a holdout A/B test); retrain monthly; monitor PSI on bill and usage Owner Retention analytics · review date 2027-02
The ₹ value rests on an assumed 30% save rate. The honest next step is an experiment: randomly hold out some high-risk customers from calls and measure the real difference in churn. Predicting churn is not the same as preventing it — the model finds who is likely to leave, not who can be persuaded to stay (that's uplift modelling).
An end-to-end ML project starts by framing the decision, capacity, costs and metrics, then explores the data, splits off an untouched test set, builds leakage-free pipelines with imputation and encoding, compares baselines and models with stratified cross-validation on ROC-AUC and PR-AUC, adds domain-driven features, tunes hyperparameters with randomised search, chooses the operating point (here the top-k call list) from out-of-fold predictions and business value, evaluates once on the test set against the current rule and random targeting, explains drivers with permutation importance, and packages the pipeline with a model card covering data, performance, value, limitations and monitoring — validating assumed impact with a controlled experiment.
7.21

Interview Questions

The questions below come up again and again in data-science and ML-engineer interviews. Each answer is written the way you'd say it: a direct answer first, then the reasoning, with the lesson to revisit. Practise answering out loud before reading.

Fundamentals

QuestionStrong answer
Explain the bias–variance trade-off.Error = bias² + variance + noise. Simple models have high bias (underfit); flexible models have high variance (overfit, sensitive to the training sample). Tune complexity with validation curves; reduce variance with more data, regularisation, bagging; reduce bias with richer models or features. (7.3)
How do you detect and prevent overfitting?Large gap between training and validation scores. Prevent with cross-validation, regularisation (L1/L2, depth limits), early stopping, more data, simpler models, ensembles, and by removing leaky features. (7.3, 7.14)
What is data leakage? Give examples.Information at training time that won't exist at prediction time: features computed after the outcome, preprocessing fitted on all data before splitting, duplicates across train/test, random splits of time series. Symptom: suspiciously good validation, poor production. (6.7, 7.14)
Why a separate validation and test set?Validation is used repeatedly to choose models and hyperparameters, so its score becomes optimistic. The test set is used once to estimate real performance. (7.3)
Parametric vs non-parametric models?Parametric models have a fixed number of parameters (linear/logistic regression); non-parametric models grow with data (KNN, decision trees). Parametric: faster, more assumptions; non-parametric: flexible, more data-hungry.

Algorithms

QuestionStrong answer
L1 vs L2 regularisation?L2 (Ridge) shrinks all weights smoothly and handles correlated features; L1 (Lasso) drives some weights to exactly zero, performing feature selection. Elastic Net combines them. Scale features first. (7.4)
Why is logistic regression a classifier if it's called "regression"?It regresses the log-odds linearly, then the sigmoid converts that to a probability; a threshold makes the class decision. Trained with log-loss. (7.5)
How does a decision tree choose splits?Greedily picks the feature/threshold that maximises impurity reduction (Gini or entropy; variance for regression). Controlled by depth, min samples per leaf, pruning. (7.11)
Random forest vs gradient boosting?Forest: deep trees in parallel on bootstrap samples with random features, averaged — reduces variance, robust with little tuning. Boosting: shallow trees in sequence fitting residuals/gradients — reduces bias, usually more accurate, needs learning rate/early stopping and more tuning. (7.12, 7.13)
XGBoost vs LightGBM vs CatBoost?All gradient-boosted trees. LightGBM: histogram + leaf-wise growth, fastest on big data. CatBoost: ordered target statistics for categoricals, strong defaults. XGBoost: mature, regularised, level-wise. Differences in accuracy are usually small. (7.13)
What is the kernel trick?Computing inner products in a high-dimensional feature space via a kernel function without building that space, letting SVMs learn non-linear boundaries (RBF, polynomial). (7.10)
Why scale features? Which models need it?Distance- and gradient-based models (KNN, SVM, logistic/linear with regularisation, PCA, neural nets) are affected by feature scale. Trees and tree ensembles are not. (6.6)
Why is Naive Bayes "naive" and why does it still work?It assumes features are independent given the class. Classification only needs the correct class to have the highest score, so ranking often survives the wrong assumption, especially in text. Probabilities are poorly calibrated. (7.9)
K-means limitations?Needs k; assumes round, similar-size clusters; sensitive to scaling, outliers and initialisation (use k-means++ and n_init). DBSCAN or Gaussian mixtures handle other shapes. (7.16)
What does PCA do and when would you avoid it?Projects standardised data onto orthogonal directions of maximum variance. Avoid when interpretability of original features matters or when the useful signal lies in low-variance directions. (7.17)

Evaluation

QuestionStrong answer
Why can accuracy be misleading?With imbalanced classes, predicting the majority class gives high accuracy and zero value. Use precision, recall, F1, PR-AUC, and cost-based evaluation. (7.6)
Precision vs recall — give a case for each.Precision when false positives are costly (blocking genuine payments, spam folder). Recall when false negatives are costly (cancer screening, fraud). (7.6)
What does ROC-AUC mean?The probability that a random positive gets a higher score than a random negative; threshold-independent ranking quality; 0.5 = random. Under heavy imbalance prefer the PR curve. (7.7)
How do you choose a classification threshold?From business costs and capacity, on validation (out-of-fold) predictions — expected value per threshold or top-k by capacity — never on the test set. (7.7, 7.20)
How do you handle class imbalance?Stratified splits, appropriate metrics, class weights / scale_pos_weight, threshold tuning, resampling (SMOTE) inside CV only, collecting more minority data. (7.6)
Which CV for time series or grouped data?TimeSeriesSplit (train on past, validate on future); GroupKFold so one customer's rows never span train and validation. (7.14)

Practice and Production

QuestionStrong answer
Walk me through an ML project you'd run.Use the 7.20 structure: business decision and metric → data and leakage check → baseline → pipeline and CV → features and tuning → threshold from business value → single test evaluation → explanation → deployment, monitoring and an experiment to confirm impact.
Your model works offline but fails in production. Why?Leakage, training/serving skew (different preprocessing), data drift or concept drift, a bug in feature pipelines, or label definition changes. Check pipelines are identical, compare feature distributions (PSI), and monitor. (7.19)
How would you explain a model to a business stakeholder?Global: permutation importance and partial dependence; local: SHAP for an individual prediction; plus examples, and performance in business units (customers saved, ₹). (7.15)
Batch vs real-time inference?Batch for scheduled decisions (cheap, simple, auditable); real-time APIs when the decision is per request in milliseconds (fraud at payment, recommendations). (7.19)
How do you pick between two models with similar scores?Check the difference is larger than CV noise; then prefer simpler, faster, more explainable, more stable, cheaper-to-serve; consider calibration and fairness across groups.

Quick-Fire Coding Check

Cell — "compute precision, recall and F1 from scratch"Python
import numpy as np
def prf(y_true, y_pred):
    y_true, y_pred = np.asarray(y_true), np.asarray(y_pred)
    tp = np.sum((y_true == 1) & (y_pred == 1)); fp = np.sum((y_true == 0) & (y_pred == 1)); fn = np.sum((y_true == 1) & (y_pred == 0))
    precision = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 0.0
    recall = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else 0.0
    f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) if precision + recall else 0.0
    return round(float(precision), 3), round(float(recall), 3), round(float(f1), 3)

from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_fscore_support
yt = [1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0]; yp = [1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0]
print("from scratch:", prf(yt, yp))
print("scikit-learn:", tuple(round(v, 3) for v in precision_recall_fscore_support(yt, yp, average="binary")[:3]))
from scratch: (0.75, 0.6, 0.667) scikit-learn: (0.75, 0.6, 0.667)
Machine learning interviews test fundamentals (bias–variance, overfitting, leakage, validation versus test sets), algorithm understanding (regularisation, logistic regression, tree splitting, bagging versus boosting, the main boosting libraries, kernels, scaling, Naive Bayes assumptions, clustering and PCA limits), evaluation (imbalance, precision versus recall, ROC-AUC versus PR-AUC, threshold choice, time-series and grouped CV) and production thinking (project walkthroughs, offline/online gaps from drift or skew, explaining models with permutation importance and SHAP, batch versus real-time inference, and choosing between similar models) — best answered with a direct answer followed by reasoning and an example.

The One Picture to Remember

Decision & metric
→
Leak-free pipeline
→
Baseline → models (CV)
→
Threshold by value
→
Test once → deploy → monitor
Machine learning covers the workflow from business framing to monitored deployment; honest evaluation with train/validation/test splits and cross-validation guided by the bias–variance trade-off; linear, logistic, KNN, Naive Bayes, SVM, tree, random-forest and gradient-boosting models; metrics matched to costs, including precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC and threshold selection; hyperparameter tuning, feature selection and interpretation; unsupervised clustering and PCA; reinforcement-learning basics; and leakage-free pipelines that are saved, served in batch or real time, and monitored for drift.
